title: He Sold Mangoes. Now He’s Trying to Archive How Humans Move.
excerpt: Raj Patel dropped out of Berkeley, used to sell mangoes, and now he’s building Human Archive, a company betting that the next great AI dataset won’t come from the internet.
author: Budera
markdown:
# He Sold Mangoes. Now He’s Trying to Archive How Humans Move.

Here’s a weird fucking founder story.

Raj Patel dropped out of Berkeley, used to sell mangoes, and now he’s building Human Archive, a company betting that the next great AI dataset won’t come from the internet.

## Before AI, There Were Mangoes

Raj and his cousin Shloke were selling mangoes long before they were building AI infrastructure. At one point, they sold 16,000 of them and planted more than 100,000 trees.

Then came Berkeley. Then dropping out. Then Human Archive.

There’s something we like about that trajectory. It doesn't feel engineered for a pitch deck. It feels like two people who keep finding weird problems and deciding to go after them.

AI has basically swallowed the internet. Books, code, images, conversations, all of it. But the physical world is still mostly undocumented. A great mechanic doesn’t just know what to do. They know how much pressure to use, what feels wrong, when to stop, how to recover when shit goes sideways.

You can't scrape that from the internet.

So Human Archive is trying to capture it. Cameras, sensors, motion, touch, real people doing real work. The goal is to turn human behavior into training data for physical AI.

It sounds simple. It’s hard.

## The Bet

If robots are going to become actual workers, someone needs to teach them what humans actually do.

Not what we say we do.

What we see, touch, move, fuck up and figure out on the fly.

Raj thinks that data is going to matter a lot.

We think the bet is fucking interesting.

The internet taught AI what humans say.

Human Archive wants to teach it what humans do.

That could end up being one hell of a dataset.

---

Budera Founder Files: interesting founders before they're obvious.

title: He Thought Remote Work Was Going to Be Shit. So He Built a Virtual Office.
excerpt: Rajiv Ayyangar had a strange idea in 2019. What if the office wasn’t a place? Then the entire fucking world went remote.
author: Budera
markdown:
# He Thought Remote Work Was Going to Be Shit. So He Built a Virtual Office.

Remote work was supposed to free everyone. Instead, it killed one of the best parts of work: being around other people. Slack gave us messages. Zoom gave us meetings. Notion gave us documents but Somehow, nobody really rebuilt the office. Rajiv Ayyangar thought that was strange. In 2019, he co-founded Tandem around a simple idea. You should be able to see who’s around, walk into a conversation, and talk without scheduling your existence three days in advance. Then COVID hit and Tandem usage jumped 30x in weeks.

The interesting part is that Rajiv wasn’t trying to build another Zoom. He was trying to rebuild the feeling of being at work. Someone’s online, so you drop by. You overhear something and join in. You want to ask a quick question without writing a paragraph in Slack. Tandem became a virtual office built around spontaneous conversation, shared screens and all the little interactions that make a team feel like a team. The idea was weird in 2019. Then suddenly the entire world was working from home.

That’s what makes Rajiv interesting. Not that he got lucky and happened to be right. He had a strong opinion before everyone else had a reason to have one. What if the office isn’t a place? Maybe that sounds obvious now. It wasn’t then. And that’s usually where the interesting founders start.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

title: They Built a Startup That Got 100,000 Users. Then They Dropped Out to Build a Robot Chef.
excerpt: Dimittri Choudhury and Alexandre Klobb had 100,000 users in six months. They still decided software wasn’t ambitious enough.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They Built a Startup That Got 100,000 Users. Then They Dropped Out to Build a Robot Chef.

Most founders would kill for 100,000 users.

Dimittri Choudhury and Alexandre Klobb got there in six months. Then they dropped out and started building a robot chef.

Their first company was essentially Duolingo for finding schools in France. It took off quickly, but the founders thought the market was moving too slowly for what they wanted to build. So they left it behind and started Mirabelle, a personal robot that takes raw ingredients, chops them, cooks them and serves dinner.

That says more about these two than any polished founder bio ever could. They aren't chasing the safest version of the future. Alexandre started freelancing at 15, moved into AI and dropped out of computer science school. Dimittri moved from a small village in France to Paris to study CS, built a startup, got traction, then decided he wanted to build something much harder.

The robot chef sounds a little ridiculous until you think about what they're actually betting on. Vision AI is finally good enough to let a machine see food, ingredients and a kitchen as something it can reason about. If it works, the payoff isn't just avoiding dinner prep. It's giving people back one of the biggest chunks of time they lose every damn day.

We like founders who make the ambitious choice when the comfortable one is already working.

They had users. They could have raised more money. They could have kept going.

Instead, they decided the next thing should be a robot in your kitchen.

That is a hell of a bet.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

title: Your Startup Doesn’t Need to Be Defensible Yet
excerpt: Founders obsess over moats when they don't even have product market fit. Someone could copy you tomorrow. Good.
author: Budera
markdown:
# Your Startup Doesn’t Need to Be Defensible Yet

Founders obsess over defensibility way too early.

Moats. Proprietary data. Network effects. Switching costs. Patents. Secret sauce. The pitch deck starts sounding like a medieval castle before anyone has even decided they want to visit the fucking place.

Your first job isn't to be impossible to copy. It's to make something people desperately want.

Someone could copy your product tomorrow. Fine. If they can, build it better. Move faster. Talk to customers. Learn things they don't know yet.

Most early startups don't have a moat. They have a handful of customers, a rough product and a founder who knows way too much about one particular problem. That's enough.

The obsession with defensibility can become an excuse to avoid the harder question. Would anyone give a shit if we disappeared tomorrow?

Because a moat around a shitty product is still a shitty product.

The best defensibility often comes later anyway. It comes from knowing the customer better, moving faster, building trust, owning distribution, collecting real data, or becoming so damn good at something that copying the feature doesn't mean copying the company.

So stop trying to build the castle before you've built the house.

Make something people want first.

Then worry about keeping it.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: Being a Founder Is Not a Personality
excerpt: The startup hoodie, the podcast, the Twitter account, the founder mode bullshit. None of it means much if you’re not actually building.
author: Budera
markdown:
# Being a Founder Is Not a Personality

The startup hoodie. The podcast. The Twitter account. The founder mode bullshit.

Somehow, entrepreneurship became its own aesthetic.

There are people who know exactly how a founder is supposed to talk, what they're supposed to post, which podcasts they're supposed to appear on, and which Silicon Valley restaurant they should probably be seen in.

Great. But none of that means you're building anything.

Being a founder is not a personality type. It is not a lifestyle. It is definitely not a fucking brand.

You're a founder because you picked something worth solving and decided to spend an unreasonable amount of your life solving it.

You don't need to look like a founder. You don't need a following. You don't need a hot take every morning. You don't need to announce that you're in founder mode.

You need customers. You need a product. You need conviction. And occasionally, you need to be stubborn enough to keep going when the whole thing looks like a terrible idea.

There is nothing wrong with talking about what you're building. Sharing the journey can be useful. A great network can change a company.

But somewhere along the way, the performance started becoming the product.

We have enough people larping entrepreneurship. We want more people actually doing it.

So stop worrying about looking like a founder.

Build something. Make it work. Get your ass kicked. Fix it. Do it again.

Stop larping. Go build.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: Is Silicon Valley Worth It Anymore?
excerpt: Silicon Valley still has the deepest founder density on earth. But does that still justify the rent, the competition, and the bullshit?
author: Budera
markdown:
# Is Silicon Valley Worth It Anymore?

For decades, the answer was obvious. If you were serious about building a technology company, you went to Silicon Valley.

You wanted engineers, you went to the Valley. You wanted investors, you went to the Valley. You wanted to meet someone who had spent ten years building exactly the thing you suddenly needed, there was probably a guy three blocks away.

That part is still true.

The weird part is that you can now build a serious company without being there.

A two person team can ship products that would have needed twenty people a few years ago. Teams are distributed. Capital is global. Your best engineer might be in Lagos, your cofounder might be in London and your customer might be in Singapore. The software doesn't give a shit where you live.

So why are founders still paying ridiculous rent to live in San Francisco?

Because Silicon Valley has something that is still brutally hard to replicate.

Density.

Founders everywhere. Engineers everywhere. Investors everywhere. Labs, weird dinners, technical meetups, accidental introductions, people changing industries over coffee. You can spend six months somewhere else trying to build a network, or walk into the right room in San Francisco and find the person who solves your problem before lunch.

That's real.

But so is the other side.

The cost of living is insane. Competition is relentless. Everyone is building something, everyone knows someone building something, and sometimes it feels like the whole place is one giant conversation about startups that never actually stops.

And there is a strange pressure to become a version of a founder that fits the Valley. Raise quickly. Hire aggressively. Talk like a VC. Build what the market understands. Optimize for the next round before you've figured out the last one.

You can lose the plot pretty fucking easily.

Maybe that's the real question.

Silicon Valley isn't dead. It is still probably the best place in the world to be if you want maximum access to the people shaping technology.

But does every founder need to be there?

Probably not.

Maybe the advantage of Silicon Valley isn't that you have to live there anymore. It's that you can go there when you need what it has.

Maybe Silicon Valley didn't stop mattering. Maybe it just stopped being mandatory.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: AI Startups Are Becoming Boring as Fuck
excerpt: Everyone is building the same agent, wrapping the same model, raising the same round, and calling it infrastructure. We think the best founders are doing something much stranger.
author: Budera
markdown:
# AI Startups Are Becoming Boring as Fuck

Everyone is building the same agent, wrapping the same model, raising the same round, and calling it infrastructure.

We get it. AI is moving fast. Models are getting better every week. There are billions of dollars flying around and nobody wants to miss the next big thing. So founders do what founders do. They look at what is working, copy the shape, add a slightly better demo and hope nobody notices how similar everything is.

The problem is that most of these companies are optimizing for what investors already understand. Another enterprise agent. Another workflow layer. Another vertical AI company with the exact same pitch deck and a different font.

And that is where things get boring.

The best companies usually look a little wrong at first. Too early. Too weird. Too hard. Too niche. Sometimes completely fucking insane.

A founder building robots instead of another AI interface. Someone attacking an industry everyone thinks is too boring for venture. A company creating an entirely new category instead of squeezing another few points out of an existing one.

Those companies are harder to pitch because there isn't already a neat box waiting for them.

Good.

Maybe we should stop asking whether a startup looks like a good investment and start asking whether it looks like something that actually needs to exist.

The next great AI company probably won't look like an AI company at all.

It'll look like something nobody has a name for yet.

And we'd much rather cover that.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: They’re Building an AI Government Affairs Firm. Seriously.
excerpt: Locke thinks government is the biggest market nobody knows how to get into. They’re trying to build the front door.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They’re Building an AI Government Affairs Firm. Seriously.

Government affairs is not exactly the first industry you think about when someone says AI startup.

That’s probably why Locke is interesting.

Founded in 2026, Locke is building an AI-native government affairs firm for companies that need to navigate regulations, lobby policymakers and win government contracts. The company combines AI agents with actual policy people who handle the relationships and the messy human parts of the job.

It sounds like a bizarre combination until you look at the problem. Government is enormous, complicated and painfully slow. There are bills, regulations, agencies, procurement rules and thousands of people making decisions that can determine whether a company gets to operate, sell or win a contract.

Locke thinks the existing system is basically the worst possible interface for getting any of this done.

Their pitch is pretty simple. Let AI handle the mountain of research, legislation, monitoring and paperwork while humans handle the relationships and strategy. The goal is not to replace the lobbyist. It is to make one lobbyist capable of doing a hell of a lot more.

The founder, Parth Badhwar, comes at this from both sides. He worked at the White House and Deloitte’s policy team before running go-to-market at a startup that sold to government offices. So he has seen the bureaucracy from the inside and the frustration from the outside.

And they’re moving fast. Locke says that just six weeks after quietly launching, it had already passed a $500K annual revenue run rate with clients across defense, healthcare and GovTech.

That’s why we’re watching it.

Not because “AI lobbying” sounds cool. It doesn’t.

Because every few years, someone looks at an industry everyone has accepted as painfully broken and says, there has to be a better fucking way to do this.

Locke is betting government affairs is one of those industries.

They might be onto something.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

title: They’re Automating the Factory Office So They Can Eventually Automate the Factory.
excerpt: Arzana started with the boring stuff manufacturers hate. Quoting, orders, invoices. The bigger bet is much more ambitious.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They’re Automating the Factory Office So They Can Eventually Automate the Factory.

Manufacturing has a funny problem. The machines are getting smarter while the people running the office are still buried in emails, PDFs, spreadsheets and the same fucking ERP they've hated for fifteen years.

Arzana is starting there.

The YC P26 startup, founded by William Alexander and Marshall Kools, builds AI agents that handle quoting, order entry, invoicing, purchasing and other repetitive work for manufacturers. The company says its customers are processing quotes and orders 10x faster, with 70% fewer data-entry errors, and has already saved customers more than $1.5 million in avoided staff costs.

That alone would make for a decent software company. But it isn't the interesting part.

Arzana wants to build the autonomous ERP for manufacturing. The current agents run the office. The long-term plan is to push those instructions onto the shop floor, eventually telling machines and robots what to produce. In other words, they're starting with the paperwork because it's the easiest place to get their foot in the door.

That's a smart place to start. Manufacturers already have the data. The workflows already exist. And the ROI is painfully obvious. If Arzana can become the system that understands what a factory has sold, ordered and promised, the jump from office execution to production execution starts looking a lot less crazy.

That's why we're watching it.

Not because another startup is putting an AI agent in an ERP.

Because they might be quietly building the software layer that connects the order a customer places to the machine that eventually makes it.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

title: They Raised $500K to Fix Lunch.
excerpt: Funch thinks lunch got way too complicated. So they’re trying to make it disappear.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They Raised $500K to Fix Lunch.

Lunch should not be this fucking complicated.

You wake up, open three delivery apps, stare at 400 options you don't want, pay too much, wait too long, and somehow end up eating the same sad chicken wrap you had yesterday. Ahmad A. and Ghada Zanaty thought there had to be a better way. So in 2025 they started Funch in Dubai around one simple idea. Pick your preferences once and let lunch just show up.

The model is deliberately boring, which is part of why it’s interesting. Funch charges AED 19 a day, has no delivery fee, and lets you skip or pause whenever you want. Behind the scenes, the company uses demand forecasting, route optimization and menu planning to make the economics work. During its early rollout, it says it delivered more than 75,000 meals with 99.8 percent delivery accuracy. It then raised $500K in pre-seed funding to scale the operation.

The bigger idea is that lunch probably shouldn't be a marketplace at all. It should be infrastructure. Funch isn't asking you to browse better. It’s trying to remove the decision entirely. That sounds almost too simple, which is usually when we start paying attention. Plenty of startups are trying to reinvent complicated industries with complicated software. Funch looked at lunch and decided the answer might just be to make the whole fucking thing disappear.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

title: He Worked in the Trades. Then Software. Now He Runs a Factory.
excerpt: Kenneth Cassel’s route to RMFG runs through the trades, software engineering and raising four kids. His next bet is a factory in Fort Worth.
author: Budera
markdown:
# He Worked in the Trades. Then Software. Now He Runs a Factory.

There is a particular kind of founder bio that makes you want to close the tab.

Kenneth Cassel’s is refreshingly fucking different.

In his public YC profile, he describes having his first kid at twenty, spending most of a decade in the trades, then stumbling into software. Four kids later, he’s building RMFG, a manufacturing company with its own factory in Fort Worth, Texas.

Sheet metal. Tubes. Machined parts. Assemblies that somebody actually needs delivered.

The interesting part is the combination. A software engineer can look at a factory and see processes to automate. Someone who has worked in the trades might also understand why those processes exist, which workarounds are essential, and which clever ideas will get laughed off the floor.

You probably want both perspectives before you start promising to reinvent manufacturing.

RMFG says it develops software to handle quoting, production scheduling and machine control inside the operation it runs. The team gets to find out whether the software works by using it to make customer orders.

That is a fairly unforgiving feedback loop. A part either fits or it doesn’t. A shipment either leaves or it doesn’t. Nobody gets extra credit because the dashboard looks expensive.

We like the shape of this bet. Own enough of the operation to learn where the actual bottlenecks are. Improve them. Make the next order easier to deliver.

Can that become a repeatable advantage as the factory takes on more complicated work? That’s the thing to watch.

For now, Cassel has picked a place where his unusual background might be useful every damn day.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

sources.title: Kenneth Cassel’s founder profile and RMFG overview

title: She Designed the Hardware. Then Went After the Tiny Defects That Ruin It.
excerpt: Erica Diaz spent years building consumer hardware. At Hundred, she’s tackling the inspection work that can quietly wreck the finished product.
author: Budera
markdown:
# She Designed the Hardware. Then Went After the Tiny Defects That Ruin It.

A tiny scratch is a stupid reason to throw away an expensive device.

It is also exactly the kind of problem that disappears when people talk about the future of manufacturing in vague, impressive sentences.

Erica Diaz has spent time closer to the problem. Her public founder profile describes years designing hardware at Meta, Google and Magic Leap, including work with manufacturing vendors in China and Mexico.

Now she’s building Hundred with Imani Gosserand and Iris Liao.

The company is developing an inspection system for consumer electronics components. Its approach uses controlled lighting and imaging to examine parts before defects get carried into a finished product.

There is something satisfying about a founder picking the thing that seems too small to headline a keynote.

Because small is relative. A cosmetic defect might be tiny. Discovering it after you have paid to assemble the rest of the device is a much bigger fucking problem.

Our read is that Diaz’s background gives this particular bet some weight. Designing hardware means making decisions that eventually have to survive suppliers, materials, tolerances and production. An image that looks good on a screen gets a very different kind of review on a factory floor.

Hundred is early. Its claims about inspection performance still need to hold up across different parts and customer conditions. We’re interested in whether the team can make adoption straightforward when a product design changes.

That is where a useful inspection tool could become part of how a factory works.

Diaz has chosen a narrow, measurable problem. You can point to the defect. You can count what slips through.

That gives the ambition somewhere concrete to start.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

title: They Met at a Research Program. Now They’re Going After Pesticides.
excerpt: Navvye Anand and Tyler Rose met at Wolfram’s summer research program. Their company, Bindwell, is taking AI into the chemistry of protecting crops.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They Met at a Research Program. Now They’re Going After Pesticides.

Pesticides are a pretty good way to make an AI conversation go quiet.

Which is partly why we’re interested.

Navvye Anand and Tyler Rose met at the Wolfram Summer Research Program in 2023. In their public launch, they describe growing up visiting farmland, leaving college, and starting Bindwell to develop new pesticides with their own AI models.

That is a fairly specific thing to decide to spend your life on.

Bindwell’s stated approach is to study proteins in harmful species and look for molecules that could target them selectively. Its research tools include Foldwell, a structure prediction model.

We’re interested in the choice of problem. A model that suggests a molecule is the beginning of a long, uncomfortable process. Someone still has to test it, understand what else it affects, and find out whether it does anything useful outside a computational prediction.

Biology doesn’t give a shit how convincing the launch video was.

That makes this a harder company to assess from the outside. We can see the founders’ stated direction. We cannot infer a successful pesticide from a protein model, and neither should anyone else.

But there’s an ambition here worth following. These two are applying their technical interests to a product whose eventual usefulness has to be measured in fields, against actual pests, under actual constraints.

The next thing we want to see is experimental evidence that moves the chemistry forward. Something a researcher can interrogate. Something a potential partner can test.

Early founders get plenty of encouragement to build whatever can be sold next month.

Anand and Rose picked pesticides.

We’d like to see where that stubbornness goes.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

sources.title: Bindwell’s founder profiles and public research launch

title: He Raced Autonomous Cars at 160 MPH. Now He Wants to Build the Factory.
excerpt: Eric Berndt’s next robotics problem is making robots in the first place. Tensr is starting with a real factory and customer orders.
author: Budera
markdown:
# He Raced Autonomous Cars at 160 MPH. Now He Wants to Build the Factory.

At 160 miles an hour, a software bug becomes a fairly physical problem.

Eric Berndt’s public profile describes racing autonomous IndyCars as a robotics researcher at Berkeley. Now he’s building Tensr with Adith Sundram and C.K. Wolfe.

The next problem they’ve chosen is the factory itself.

Tensr says it operates a 12,000-square-foot facility in the Bay Area manufacturing robots for customers. Its longer-term goal is to automate more of the path from a new order to production.

That is a useful place to put an ambitious robotics team. Every robot company eventually has to confront the awkward difference between building one machine and delivering a batch that works.

Parts have to arrive. Assemblies need to be consistent. A design revision has to make it onto the floor without turning everyone’s week into a complete fucking mess.

We like that Berndt and his co-founders have put those problems at the centre of the company. A factory serving other hardware teams has a reason to learn from more than one product and more than one customer’s mistakes.

Whether those lessons can become reusable automation is the big question. Manufacturing different things can also mean absorbing a fresh set of complications with every order.

So we’re watching for repeatability. Does the next build get easier? Do changeovers improve? Can the team take on new work without starting the whole process again?

Those are less exciting questions than how fast an autonomous race car can go.

They might be the questions that decide how many useful robots get built.

Berndt has gone from pushing a machine around a track to trying to change the place machines come from.

That’s a hell of a second act to attempt.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

sources.title: Tensr’s founders, factory and manufacturing thesis

title: A Pretty AI Dress Is Easy. She Wants One a Factory Can Actually Make.
excerpt: Yuliya Raquel is building PatternFast around the awkward journey from a clothing idea to patterns, sizing and production instructions.
author: Budera
markdown:
# A Pretty AI Dress Is Easy. She Wants One a Factory Can Actually Make.

The internet can generate a beautiful jacket in seconds.

Try asking the image where the fucking seams go.

That’s the territory Yuliya Raquel is working in. After founding Tailornova/Couturme, she’s building PatternFast, a company focused on turning clothing ideas into the information needed to manufacture them.

In its public launch, PatternFast describes tools for garment patterns, sizing, fabric adjustments and production documentation.

It’s easy to miss how much of the product lives in those details. A design needs to fit a body. Different fabrics stretch differently. One sample needs to become a range of sizes that still looks like the same garment.

These are the kinds of problems you can edit out of a demo and immediately encounter when you try to make something.

What interests us about Raquel is the persistence of the subject. The public history runs through more than one company name, but the work keeps returning to the connection between design and manufacturing.

That suggests a deeper question than whether AI can draw clothes. Can software carry more of a designer’s intention into something that can be cut, sewn and sold?

We’re treating PatternFast’s speed and savings claims as company claims. The test we care about is whether production teams can use the output with less correction and fewer rounds of sampling.

A factory-ready pattern is a demanding promise. There are people downstream who will discover very quickly whether it is true.

Raquel has picked a problem with that kind of accountability built in.

The generated image gets the attention. The person who makes it possible to produce the garment might build the more useful company.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

sources.title: Yuliya Raquel’s profile and PatternFast’s production workflow

title: His Big Manufacturing Bet Is a Room Full of Flies.
excerpt: Keiran Olivares Whitaker’s Entocycle builds technology for insect farming. The interesting work is making the biology behave like an operation.
author: Budera
markdown:
# His Big Manufacturing Bet Is a Room Full of Flies.

There are easier things to explain at dinner than your insect factory.

Keiran Olivares Whitaker picked that conversation anyway.

He founded Entocycle, which develops technology and facilities for farming black soldier flies. The basic idea is to use insects to turn organic waste into useful products, including protein for animal feed.

Entocycle’s London demonstration facility combines computer vision, climate control, automation and data collection around a live colony.

That combination is what interests us. Biology gives you an astonishing little conversion machine. Building a business means getting it to perform consistently, in large numbers, under conditions you can afford to maintain.

The insects do not read your operating plan. They do not care that a buyer wants a delivery on Tuesday. You have to understand the process well enough to make a dependable operation around them.

That’s a properly difficult engineering problem hiding inside a story people might dismiss as weird food tech.

Our read is that Whitaker’s company sits in a useful place: the machinery and operational knowledge other insect producers need. If more people want to produce this kind of feed, someone has to make the farm work.

The economics still matter. Waste inputs, operating costs, product consistency and what a customer will actually pay are going to decide much more than a sustainability slogan.

We want to see whether Entocycle can help operators produce reliably enough to earn repeat business.

But we like a founder willing to spend years inside the unglamorous part of an unusual idea.

Some people see a room full of flies and leave.

Whitaker saw something worth engineering.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

title: She’s Building a Business Around the Crops That Don’t Get Sold.
excerpt: Nidhi Pant and the S4S Technologies team connect food preservation equipment with a route to market. The dryer is only part of the idea.
author: Budera
markdown:
# She’s Building a Business Around the Crops That Don’t Get Sold.

Growing food and getting paid for it are two very different problems.

Nidhi Pant is working on the gap between them.

She’s a co-founder of S4S Technologies, which provides solar-powered dryers and food processing equipment to rural communities in India. The company also connects preserved food products with commercial buyers.

That second part deserves more attention.

A useful machine can still leave someone with a new problem. Congratulations, your tomatoes last longer. Who buys them? In what form? How do you get a reliable order instead of another pile of stock waiting for a customer?

According to the Earthshot Prize’s account of S4S, the model includes helping women farmers and entrepreneurs preserve produce and sell products made from it. S4S won the prize’s waste category in 2023.

We’re interested in the operational choice underneath the award. The team has taken responsibility for more of the journey from crop to income.

That sounds obvious until you look at how many startups would prefer to ship the clever bit and leave distribution to somebody else.

It also makes the business harder. Equipment, training, quality and buyers have to line up. The system needs to keep working when the weather changes or the next harvest looks different.

Our view is that founders who stay with those details can learn things a more distant competitor will struggle to see. The opportunity is in knowing how the whole transaction actually happens.

Pant’s work is a reminder that a big idea can start with a very practical question.

There is food here. Someone could use it. How do we make sure the person who grew it gets paid?

That is worth a founder’s time.

Budera Founder Files. The people building before the rest of us know what to call it.

sources.title: The Earthshot Prize’s account of S4S Technologies

title: The Robot Arm Is Already There. They’re Teaching It to Find the Weld.
excerpt: Forge Robotics is starting with vision and welding in metal fabrication. Its larger ambition begins with making existing arms more useful.
author: Budera
markdown:
# The Robot Arm Is Already There. They’re Teaching It to Find the Weld.

A robot arm that needs a specialist every time the part changes comes with a fairly important asterisk.

Forge Robotics is going after that asterisk.

The early company is developing vision and control technology for metal fabrication, starting with welding. In its public launch, Forge describes a robot-mounted vision system that maps the work, identifies seams and guides the arm.

That gives us a specific reason to pay attention. The workpiece is real. It might arrive slightly different from the last one. The system has to figure out where the useful action should happen.

There is a lot more to a good weld than finding a line, of course. Fit-up, materials, access and process quality all matter. Seeing the seam is part of a much larger job.

Forge’s ambition is to extend into more of the fabrication process. We’re reading that as a roadmap. What matters first is whether the initial system can handle customer parts reliably enough to justify its place in a shop.

That’s the stage we like to watch. Before a company gets to turn a narrow success into a giant story, it has to earn the success.

The interesting upside is practical. If changing the work takes less specialist programming, robotic welding could make sense for more of the jobs a fabricator actually receives.

More useful hours from equipment. Less time teaching the same arm what changed.

We’ll be watching the gap between a controlled demonstration and a shop with awkward parts, deadlines and people who have heard plenty of automation promises already.

Forge has chosen a problem where those people can tell you very quickly whether you’ve built something worth a damn.

title: Their Robot’s First Interesting Job Is Packing Little Chemical Vials.
excerpt: Verne Robotics says it deployed a two-arm robot to pack vials at ABClonal. We’re interested in how much work sits between unpacking and useful output.
author: Budera
markdown:
# Their Robot’s First Interesting Job Is Packing Little Chemical Vials.

Packing chemical vials probably won’t get a standing ovation at a technology conference.

We’d still rather hear about the job.

Verne Robotics, founded by Neil Nie and Aditya Jha, is developing robot arms that learn manipulation tasks from demonstrations. Its public launch describes Nemo3, a two-arm system, and a deployment packing vials at ABClonal.

The company says it went from unpacking to automating that task in four days. That is its account, and the setup time is exactly the part we would want to examine with a customer.

Because getting the robot to do something once is a very different expense from getting it to do something usefully every day.

There is the demonstration data. The workspace. The objects. The handoff when a person needs to intervene. The changes a customer makes after you thought you’d finished.

Verne also describes an hourly payment model. That creates an interesting commercial question: can the team get a robot working quickly enough, and keep it productive long enough, to make the economics work for both sides?

That’s a much more useful question than how many tasks a model can theoretically learn.

Our read is that a narrow packaging job is a sensible place to test the larger ambition. A customer has an existing process and a reason to compare results.

We want to see what happens on the next deployment. Does the learning carry over? Does support become easier? How often does the workflow change?

Tiny vials. Repeated movements. A very specific piece of work.

There are worse places to start finding out whether flexible robotics can become a business.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

title: They Want a Robot to Deal With Your Old Laptop.
excerpt: Revise Robotics is working on the awkward middle of electronics resale: testing, wiping, documenting and preparing used machines for another owner.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They Want a Robot to Deal With Your Old Laptop.

Your old laptop might still be useful.

Unfortunately, somebody has to find out what’s wrong with it first.

Then wipe it. Test it. Work out what it is. Photograph it. Get it ready for someone who expects the damn thing to work when it arrives.

Revise Robotics is building automation for that process.

Founded by Rupesh Jeyaram and Antonio Monreal, the company describes a robotic system for electronics refurbishment facilities, starting with laptops. Its stated workflow includes testing devices, wiping storage, photographing them and creating resale listings.

We like this because the work already has a purpose. There’s a device at one end and a potential second owner at the other. The middle is a collection of physical and digital tasks that somebody has to complete.

It is also messy in ways a polished demo can conceal. Different models. Different operating systems. Missing information. Machines that have spent years acquiring problems their manufacturers didn’t plan for.

Revise’s public launch described an initial pilot. That is an early milestone, and we’re treating the broader automation claims as something the team still has to demonstrate across real inventories.

The question we care about is whether it improves the economics per device. How much can the system process, how much intervention does it need, and how confidently can the next buyer trust the result?

If those answers improve, more devices might be worth putting back into circulation.

There’s a whole robotics story hiding in the pile of equipment someone else decided to get rid of.

Revise is choosing to look through it.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

sources.title: Revise Robotics’ workflow, founders and pilot announcement

title: Their Robotics Pitch Starts With Getting Through the Shift.
excerpt: Ultra is building robots for repetitive industrial work. We’re watching whether quick setup and flexible tasks can survive a customer’s working day.
author: Budera
markdown:
# Their Robotics Pitch Starts With Getting Through the Shift.

The future of robotics gets discussed in some very large rooms.

The purchase decision might happen next to a conveyor belt.

Ultra is building robots for repetitive industrial tasks. Its founding team includes people who previously built Layer By Layer and Voodoo Manufacturing, and its public profile says it already has robots in the field generating revenue.

The company’s pitch emphasises fast installation and the ability to learn new tasks. Those are company claims. They’re also sensible things for a customer to care about.

An operations team has to fit the machine into an existing day. There is space to find, work to assign, people to train and an exception that will arrive as soon as everyone thinks the setup is finished.

Making that manageable might be just as valuable as making the robot more capable.

Our interest is in the accumulated experience behind the team’s choice. Building manufacturing companies gives you opportunities to discover how much work happens around the equipment. The handoffs and interruptions can decide whether a technically impressive system gets used.

That doesn’t prove Ultra has solved deployment. It gives us a reason to follow how it approaches the problem.

We’d want to see a customer change a task. Watch what happens when the line stops. Understand who supports the robot when the founding team is somewhere else.

Those details are where a flexible system earns the description.

For now, Ultra has picked an appropriately demanding audience: people who need work completed before the shift ends.

They are unlikely to accept a nice video as payment for the interruption.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

sources.title: Ultra’s product approach and founding team

title: They’re Putting Solar-Powered Compute on the Water.
excerpt: NetworkOcean’s latest bet is floating solar data centres. The early question is how quickly a strange-looking system can serve a real workload.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They’re Putting Solar-Powered Compute on the Water.

Somewhere in the journey from an AI idea to a running workload, somebody needs to provide electricity.

NetworkOcean has taken that requirement in a fairly unusual direction.

The company, founded by Sam Mendel and Eric Kim, is developing floating solar data centres. In its latest public launch, the team says it ran a customer AI workload on an H100 powered by solar on the water, going from paper to deployment in 53 days.

That is the company’s account of an early demonstration. It does not establish the economics of a large data centre.

It does give us a concrete reason to look closer.

The proposed advantage is getting compute and power working together faster. It is an infrastructure bet about what has to happen before the model gets to run at all.

The awkward questions arrive immediately. What happens overnight? How do maintenance and connectivity work? What does the installation cost once you include the whole system? Which water sites actually make sense?

Good. A strange idea should survive specific questions.

We’re interested in whether the team can turn an initial workload into a repeatable installation customers want to use. The useful comparison is the full cost and time required to deliver dependable compute.

We also like that the public story has changed from an earlier underwater data centre concept to the current floating solar approach. The details of the implementation matter more than loyalty to the first pitch.

There is plenty here left to prove.

But a small team putting a real workload on an unusual source of infrastructure is exactly the sort of thing we want to notice while it still looks a little odd.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

sources.title: NetworkOcean’s current floating solar launch and earlier concept

title: They Want to Automate the Excavator You Already Own.
excerpt: Flywheel AI is starting with remote control for existing excavators and using the work to collect data for future autonomy.
author: Budera
markdown:
# They Want to Automate the Excavator You Already Own.

An excavator is an expensive thing to replace just because someone has a new software idea.

Flywheel AI is starting with the machine already on the site.

The early team is developing retrofit equipment and remote controls for excavators. In its public launch, it describes using teleoperated work to collect data for automating construction tasks over time.

There is a practical sequence here that we like. Get access to the machine. Make remote operation useful. Learn from the work that actually happens.

Each step has to earn the right to lead to the next one.

A remote control system has its own demanding requirements. Operators need to understand what is happening around the machine. Supervisors need a way to take over. A connection problem cannot become everyone else’s emergency.

Flywheel describes controls and intervention features in its launch. We’d want to see how they perform under customer conditions before drawing conclusions about deployment readiness.

The autonomy part is a further ambition. Collecting data from a task does not automatically produce a system that can perform it safely on its own.

Still, there’s something useful about building around existing equipment. Contractors have already made a major investment. A product that improves that equipment has a different route into the operation from one that asks them to buy a whole new fleet.

We’re watching for evidence that operators want to keep using it after the first trial, and for a clear account of which tasks become automated next.

There is a lot of future to talk about in construction robotics.

Flywheel is starting by getting its hands on the controls.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

sources.title: Flywheel AI’s retrofit, remote operation and data collection approach

title: A Classics Major and a Mechanical Engineer Are Building Drone Submarines.
excerpt: Albacore is working on long-range unmanned underwater vehicles. We’re interested in the manufacturing problem underneath the ambitious pitch.
author: Budera
markdown:
# A Classics Major and a Mechanical Engineer Are Building Drone Submarines.

An underwater robot makes it very easy to say something that sounds impressive.

Try producing enough of them, keeping them working and getting them where they’re needed.

Albacore, founded by Dante Vaisbort and John Huddleston, is developing long-range drone submarines. Its public materials put manufacturing at the centre of the pitch: underwater systems designed to be produced in volume.

The founders have an unusual combination of backgrounds. Vaisbort studied classics before building defence technology companies. Huddleston is a mechanical engineer who worked on autonomous systems and manufacturing advisory projects.

The company’s claims about vehicle capability are its own. We’re interested in the questions behind those claims rather than treating a launch description as an operational record.

What can the team build consistently? How much testing does each vehicle require? What happens when something needs servicing? Does producing more units make the system easier to support or multiply the problems?

That is a substantial part of the robotics business in any environment. Underwater, the consequences of getting the details wrong are particularly unforgiving.

Our read is that the manufacturing emphasis makes Albacore worth following. There is a big difference between a successful prototype and a product an organisation can procure, operate and maintain repeatedly.

We want to see evidence that the team can close that distance.

The ocean gives this story its scale. The less glamorous work of parts, production and support will probably decide how far it goes.

A small company has decided to take all of that on.

That’s enough to get it onto our watchlist. Now it has to build.

Budera Worth Watching. The companies we think you’ll wish you found earlier.

sources.title: Albacore’s public company launch and founder backgrounds

title: Your Robot Demo Should Come With the Rest of the Shift.
excerpt: The useful part of a robotics demo might be what happened in the seven hours nobody filmed. Show us the interruptions.
author: Budera
markdown:
# Your Robot Demo Should Come With the Rest of the Shift.

Show us the part after the robot picks up the object.

The next object. The one after that. The one somebody put down slightly wrong. The interruption. The restart. The person who has to walk over and fix whatever just happened.

Then keep the camera running.

We like a good demo. Watching a machine do something difficult is exciting. There is real engineering in making the first successful attempt happen, and people deserve credit for it.

But a buyer is trying to understand a working day.

How much useful work gets completed? What needs resetting? How long does recovery take? Does the operator end up spending the afternoon babysitting the thing that was supposed to free up their time?

Those questions can make an impressive system look very different.

They also create an opportunity for a less impressive-looking machine. A robot doing a narrow job reliably can be extremely valuable to the person responsible for that job.

Founders should get more comfortable showing the messy version. Explain what failed. Say where a person helped. Show the conditions under which the system works and what you’re improving next.

That gives a customer something to evaluate. It gives the engineering progress some context. It might even make the successful part more impressive because we understand what it took.

There’s plenty of room for ambition. We just want a clearer account of the work between the highlights.

Make the beautiful clip.

Then tell us how the rest of the shift went.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: If Your Market Sounds Boring at Dinner, You Might Be Onto Something.
excerpt: There are customers with expensive problems in industries that will never make you sound cool. That should be encouraging.
author: Budera
markdown:
# If Your Market Sounds Boring at Dinner, You Might Be Onto Something.

Somewhere, a founder is trying to make a genuinely useful company sound more interesting to someone who will never buy the product.

Stop doing that.

If you fix inspection paperwork, sell the inspection paperwork. If you help a factory quote jobs, talk about the factory. If the exciting part of the week is that an order went out correctly, explain why that matters.

The customer already knows.

They know how much time the problem eats. They know who gets called when it breaks. They might have spent years assuming that this particular piece of their working life was going to stay annoying forever.

That is a pretty good place to start a conversation.

You still need a business. A boring market can have terrible margins, slow purchasing and customers who have no budget. Obscurity doesn’t magically make the economics work.

But neither does a fashionable category.

We’d rather see a founder understand one expensive problem in uncomfortable detail than collect the right words to describe a giant opportunity they’ve barely touched.

Who pays? Why now? How do they do the job today? What would make switching worthwhile? Answer those and your company starts getting interesting very quickly.

You can find plenty of ambition inside an unglamorous first product. The founder who knows the workflow might see an entire operation that could work better.

They just have somewhere specific to begin.

Let the dinner conversation be boring.

Build the thing the customer calls you about on Monday.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: A Pilot Is a Question. Stop Announcing It Like an Answer.
excerpt: A company agreeing to try your product is useful. The real learning is what makes them pay, renew and bring it into the work.
author: Budera
markdown:
# A Pilot Is a Question. Stop Announcing It Like an Answer.

We’ve signed a pilot.

Great. What are you trying to find out?

Because that is the useful part. A pilot gives you a chance to test whether your product belongs inside someone else’s operation. You get access, attention and a set of real constraints that your own team probably couldn’t invent.

Treat that as something precious.

Agree on the job. Agree on what a successful result looks like. Work out who has the authority and budget to do something if it succeeds.

Otherwise you can spend months performing helpful little experiments for a company that likes you and has absolutely no plan to buy.

That happens easily. The person running the trial might be enthusiastic. The users might have good feedback. Everyone might enjoy the meetings.

Then you ask what happens next and discover that nobody has thought about it.

A founder needs to ask earlier.

What would make this worth paying for? Which existing cost or constraint changes? What has to happen before the product becomes part of the normal workflow?

Those questions can feel less comfortable than announcing another logo.

Good. They give the pilot a purpose.

We like early traction. We also want to know what it represents. A trial, a paid deployment, a renewal and an expanding account tell you different things about a company.

Founders should be specific about which one they have.

The pilot is where you earn the evidence for the next claim.

Get the evidence. Then make the claim.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: Put the Human in the Diagram.
excerpt: If someone is still helping your AI complete the job, explain their role. The handoff might be one of the most important parts of the product.
author: Budera
markdown:
# Put the Human in the Diagram.

If a person steps in when your system gets stuck, put them in the diagram.

Tell the customer what they do. Explain when they get called. Account for their time in the price.

This should be a perfectly normal product conversation.

Early systems often need help. Sometimes the useful version of a product will continue to need help, because the job includes exceptions that are expensive or pointless to automate completely.

The founder’s job is to understand that boundary.

How often does an exception happen? Can the person see enough context to handle it? Does their intervention let the system continue, or do they end up doing the entire task themselves?

Those details determine what the customer is buying.

They also determine whether the business can grow. An operation that requires more human attention with every deployment has a different cost structure from one where the same support team can handle more work over time.

Both deserve to be measured properly.

We get suspicious when the human help disappears from the pitch but remains essential to the result. That makes it harder to understand the product, the economics and what progress actually means.

Show the handoff. Improve it. Give the operator a decent interface. Make recovery faster. Learn which situations keep causing problems.

There is serious engineering in that work.

A customer can make an informed decision about a system that needs occasional assistance.

They’ll have a much harder time trusting one that made the assistance a surprise.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: Your First Ten Customers Should Probably Look Embarrassingly Similar.
excerpt: A product for everyone can give an early team ten completely different jobs. Find a group whose problems let the work compound.
author: Budera
markdown:
# Your First Ten Customers Should Probably Look Embarrassingly Similar.

Here is a version of early traction that can quietly fuck up a company.

Ten customers. Ten industries. Ten workflows. Ten sets of custom requirements that all seem reasonable in the meeting.

The slide looks great. The engineering calendar looks like a hostage note.

An early team needs learning that carries over. The next customer should help you understand the same problem more deeply, rather than introduce an entirely new profession you now have to master.

That usually means being more specific about who you serve.

Which job do they need done? What tools do they already use? What do they consider a good result? Who signs off when it works?

If those answers keep changing, you might be collecting projects faster than you’re building a product.

Projects can pay the bills. They can teach you useful things. Just be honest about the work you are taking on and what you expect to reuse.

We like founders who can describe the next customer in detail. They know where to find them. They know which complaint will start the conversation. They’ve already seen enough of the workflow to anticipate the awkward questions.

That kind of focus can look small from a distance.

Up close, it gives the company a chance to get better with every deployment. Sales gets clearer. Setup gets easier. The product starts arriving with answers instead of another list of things to build.

There will be time to widen the market.

First, find a group of people whose problems let you learn the same lesson more than once.

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.

title: You Raised Money. Tell Us What You Can Do With It.
excerpt: The interesting part of a funding round is the work it makes possible. Start there and the announcement might actually be worth reading.
author: Budera
markdown:
# You Raised Money. Tell Us What You Can Do With It.

Congratulations on the round.

Now tell us what changes on Monday.

Can you run an experiment you couldn’t afford? Build a second machine? Hire the person who understands the part of the problem your team keeps getting wrong?

Can a customer finally get the thing they’ve been waiting for?

That is the interesting story.

Funding announcements have a habit of treating the money as the result. The amount gets the headline. The investor list takes a lap. Somebody explains that the market is enormous and the team is uniquely positioned.

By the end, we still don’t know what the company is going to build.

A useful announcement could be much simpler. Here is the constraint we hit. Here is what the capital lets us attempt. Here is what we need to learn before the next stage makes sense.

That would also make the ambition easier to believe. A founder who can describe the next difficult milestone probably understands more than one who can only describe the eventual market size.

And sometimes the milestone is unglamorous. Getting manufacturing consistent. Reducing the time required to onboard a customer. Making support work without the founder answering every message.

Those can be the things that let a company grow.

We’re happy founders get the resources to keep going. Building is expensive, uncertainty is real and a little breathing room can change what a team is able to attempt.

We just want to hear about the attempt.

You got the money. What does it let you make possible?

Budera Hot Takes. Strong opinions from people actually paying attention.
